paragraphes: At school, you follow rules. No phones in class. Be on time. Hand in your homework.
Your sports club has other rules. Your family has rules too.
You must learn the rules that apply to you, then follow them. For a company, this is called compliance.

decouverte.comme: Every place has a rulebook: school, club, home. To be in line, you must know which rulebooks are yours. Then you must follow them.
decouverte.enVrai: A company has many kinds of rules. There are laws, regulations (detailed rules from the government), industry standards (rules for one type of business), and contracts (written deals). Compliance means finding all these rules and meeting them. The picture stops here: at school, a teacher reminds you. A company must find its own rules.

decouverte.question: A company follows every security rule that applies to it. Is it fully safe?
options: Yes, following the rules is enough
No, it is a good base, but only a first step
Yes, if an inspector checked it
decouverte.answer: No, it is a good base, but only a first step
decouverte.explanation: The manual says compliance is a solid base, but only the first step. Rules can leave weak points. The other two answers are tempting, but they are not right.

decouverte.texte: An online shop sells clothes. It follows the law on its customers' data, like names and addresses. It follows the rules for card payments. It keeps the promises in its contracts with suppliers. That is three kinds of rules for one shop.

decouverte.comme: The pass mark is the minimum to move up a year. It does not mean you know the whole course.
decouverte.enVrai: Being compliant means you reached the minimum. To be really protected, you often need more. Compliance is a starting point, not the finish line.

cards.question: Official definition: “compliance”
cards.answer: (ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.
cards.explanation: In simple words: compliance means a company finds out all the rules that apply to it, and really follows them. Adherence means sticking to a rule. A mandate is a duty.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Determine Compliance and Other Requirements”. (ISC)2 is the group that gives the CISSP certificate.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “compliance”?
options: (ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws and regulatory requirements.

(ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.

(ISC)2 defines compliance as awareness of a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.

(ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and test all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.
options_why: This sentence forgets two kinds of rules: industry standards and contractual agreements.
Awareness only means knowing the rule. The real word is adherence: you must also follow it.
The company must satisfy the rules, not only test them.
cards.answer: (ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: adherence to a mandate, understand and satisfy, and the four kinds of rules.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “compliance” from memory.
cards.answer: (ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.
cards.explanation: Three ideas: stick to a duty, understand and meet every rule, and cover laws, standards, and contracts.

cards.question: A company followed every rule in its rulebooks. What does the manual say about its security?
options: It is now fully safe from every kind of attack
It can stop reviewing its security now
It has no security work left to do
A solid base, but only a first step
options_why: Rules cannot cover every attack. A weak point can stay even when every box is ticked.
Rules and attacks both change, so the company must keep checking.
Compliance is only the first step. More work is needed to be really secure.
cards.answer: A solid base, but only a first step
cards.explanation: Compliance is a good starting point. Real security often means going further.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”. The manual calls compliance a solid baseline and only the first step.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a source of compliance rules?
options: A coworker's personal opinion about security
A law passed to protect customers' personal data
A contract that a supplier signed with the company
A standard written for one type of industry
options_why: Laws are a main source of compliance rules.
Contractual agreements are part of the definition.
Industry standards are one of the four kinds of rules.
cards.answer: A coworker's personal opinion about security
cards.explanation: The four kinds are laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contracts. An opinion is not one of them.

cards.question: A company finds all the rules that apply to it, then follows them. What is this called?
options: Integrity
Encryption
Compliance
Availability
options_why: Integrity means data stays correct. It is not about following rules.
Encryption scrambles data. It is one tool, not the whole effort.
Availability means systems can be used when needed. It is a different goal.
cards.answer: Compliance
cards.explanation: Compliance means understanding the rules and meeting them.

cards.question: A bank and a school do not follow exactly the same compliance rules. Why?
options: Each manager chooses the rules for his company
Only banks have to follow laws
The bank's rules are always twice as strict
Some rules apply to only certain industries
options_why: Managers do not pick the rules. Laws, standards, and contracts set them.
Laws apply broadly to all industries, so schools follow laws too.
The manual says nothing like this. The real reason is that some rules fit one industry only.
cards.answer: Some rules apply to only certain industries
cards.explanation: Some rules apply to all industries. Others are only for certain industries or products.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: A new manager starts the compliance work of a company. What should she do FIRST?
options: Find out which laws, standards, and contracts apply
Buy new security tools for the whole network
Ask all of the staff to sign a new policy
Test the network to look for weak points
options_why: Tools may help later. But she cannot pick the right ones before she knows the rules.
A policy comes after the manager knows which rules it must cover.
Testing is useful, but it does not tell her which rules apply.
cards.answer: Find out which laws, standards, and contracts apply
cards.explanation: The definition starts with understanding. You must know the rules before you can satisfy them.

cards.question: A company passed all its compliance checks. The manager says that the company is now fully secure. What is the BEST response?
options: Agree, because the rules cover every possible attack
Compliance is a good base, but more work is needed
Agree, and stop all future security reviews
Disagree, because compliance has no value for security
options_why: Rules cannot cover every attack. Attackers do not read rulebooks.
Rules and attacks change. Reviews must continue.
This is too extreme. The manual calls compliance a solid baseline.
cards.answer: Compliance is a good base, but more work is needed
cards.explanation: Compliance is a solid base, but only the first step toward being secure.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Rules and attacks both change over time. Which action is MOST useful for a company's compliance?
options: Check the rules once, when the company starts
Wait for an outside inspector to find problems
Review its practices on a regular basis
Follow only the rules that cost very little
options_why: The set of rules keeps changing, so one check is not enough.
Waiting is reactive. The manual asks for a continuous review.
The company must satisfy all applicable rules, not only the cheap ones.
cards.answer: Review its practices on a regular basis
cards.explanation: The expectations keep changing. So the practices need a continuous review.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: A supplier contract says the company must encrypt all customer data. Which kind of requirement is this?
options: A law passed by the government
A contractual agreement
A tip that staff can ignore
A standard written for the whole industry
options_why: Laws come from a government. This duty comes from a signed deal.
A contract term is a duty. Ignoring it can break the deal.
An industry standard is shared by many companies. This one is a deal between two parties.
cards.answer: A contractual agreement
cards.explanation: Contractual agreements are one of the four kinds of rules that compliance covers.

cards.question: Which statement about compliance is NOT correct?
options: It needs a continuous review of practices
It includes understanding and meeting contracts
It is a solid base for security
Being compliant is the same as being secure
options_why: This is true. Rules keep changing, so the company must keep reviewing.
This is true. Contractual agreements are in the definition.
This is true. The manual calls it a solid baseline.
cards.answer: Being compliant is the same as being secure
cards.explanation: Compliance is only the first step toward security. Many people mix up the two.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: A worker says that the law is enough, so a contract rule can be ignored. What is the BEST answer?
options: No: contracts are part of compliance too
Yes: laws are the only rules that matter
Yes: contracts are only friendly advice
No: contracts matter only for big companies
options_why: The definition lists four kinds of rules, and contracts are one of them.
A contract is a legal deal. Breaking it has consequences.
Contracts apply to companies of any size.
cards.answer: No: contracts are part of compliance too
cards.explanation: Compliance covers laws, regulations, industry standards, and contractual agreements.

cards.question: What is the difference between compliance and security?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Security means meeting rules; compliance means buying tools
Compliance means meeting rules; security often needs more
Compliance gives stronger protection than security
options_why: Many people mix them up, but the manual says they are not the same.
It is the other way round. Compliance is about meeting rules.
No: compliance is only a baseline, so security usually needs more.
cards.answer: Compliance means meeting rules; security often needs more
cards.explanation: Meeting the rules is the first step. Being secure often means doing more.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: In your own words: why must a company review its compliance often?
cards.answer: Rules change, and so do attacks. What was fine last year may not be fine now. So the company must check again and again.
cards.explanation: The manual says the expectations keep changing and need a continuous review.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: What does “adherence to a mandate” mean?
cards.answer: Sticking to a duty: not only knowing it, but really following it.
cards.explanation: Adherence means sticking to the rule. A mandate is an order or a duty.

cards.question: A colleague says: “We are compliant, so we are safe.” What do you answer?
cards.answer: Compliance is a solid base, but only the first step. A company can follow every rule and still have weak points.
cards.explanation: Think of the pass mark: it lets you move up, but it does not prove you know everything.

cards.question: Name two topics covered by the laws that a CISSP must know.
cards.answer: For example: cybercrime, data leaks, rights over ideas, import and export rules, data moving between countries, and privacy.
cards.explanation: You will meet these topics in the next galaxies.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Legal and Regulatory Issues”.

paragraphes: Julie spends a week at a school in another country. She uses her phone in class, like at home.
The teacher takes it away. At this school, phones are banned. The rules of her own school do not count here.
Who has the power to make rules in a place? This question is called jurisdiction.

decouverte.titre: Each place has its own head teacher
decouverte.comme: Each school has a head teacher. The head teacher decides for that school, not for the school next door.
decouverte.enVrai: A jurisdiction is the official power to make legal decisions in an area. A company can be under several jurisdictions at once. The picture stops here: a student has only one head teacher.

decouverte.question: An online shop in one country sells to customers in another country. Who may have a say over its rules?
options: Only the shop's country
Maybe both countries, depending on treaties and on what the shop does
Only the customers' country
decouverte.answer: Maybe both countries, depending on treaties and on what the shop does
decouverte.explanation: A map is not enough. Treaties (official agreements between countries) and what the company does also count.

decouverte.texte: A payment company has its main office in one country. Its servers are in a second country. Its customers live in ten other countries. Several officials may say: “Here, you follow our rules.” So experts do not only look at the map.

cards.question: Official definition: “jurisdiction”
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: In simple words: jurisdiction is the official power to make legal decisions and judgments in an area. It tells you who can set rules for you.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “jurisdiction”?
options: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to enforce company policies.
Jurisdiction is a geographic concept that establishes the borders where legal decisions and judgments are made.
Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments only inside one country.
Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
options_why: Jurisdiction is about legal power, not about company policies.
Jurisdiction is a legal concept about official power. A map is not enough.
Jurisdiction is not limited to one country. Treaties and the company's activity can also play a part.
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: legal concept, official power, and legal decisions and judgments.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “jurisdiction” from memory.
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a legal concept, an official power, and legal decisions and judgments.

cards.question: What is the FIRST challenge in finding a company's compliance requirements?
options: Knowing who has the legal power to set them
Choosing which security software to buy first
Writing a new security policy for all offices
Training all staff on how to spot attacks
options_why: Software comes later. First the company must know which rules apply.
A policy is written after the requirements are known.
Training is useful, but it is a later step.
cards.answer: Knowing who has the legal power to set them
cards.explanation: Before you read the rules, you must know which jurisdiction has the right to set them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: An online shop sells in two countries. What can decide which rules it must follow?
options: Only the country in which its head office sits
The map, treaties, and what the shop does
Only the language that its customers speak
Only the number of pages on its website
options_why: The manual says geography alone is not enough.
Language has no legal power. Authorities do.
The size of a website does not decide who has legal power.
cards.answer: The map, treaties, and what the shop does
cards.explanation: Jurisdiction can also depend on international treaties and on the activity of the organization.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”. The manual says it is not enough to know the geography or political boundaries.

cards.question: Is the map enough to know a company's jurisdiction?
options: Yes: the home country settles every question
Yes, but only for small companies
No: treaties and activity can also matter
No: only the customers' choice matters
options_why: The manual says geography and borders are not enough.
Size does not change this. Treaties and activity can matter for every company.
Customers do not choose the legal power. Authorities and treaties do.
cards.answer: No: treaties and activity can also matter
cards.explanation: Geography is one part. Treaties and the company's activity count too.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: A company sells in three countries. Does it have only one jurisdiction?
options: Yes: a company always has exactly one jurisdiction
Not always: it can fall under several at once
Yes: the one chosen by its first customer
No: it has none until a court says so
options_why: A company can answer to several authorities at once.
Customers do not choose the jurisdiction.
Jurisdiction exists before any court case.
cards.answer: Not always: it can fall under several at once
cards.explanation: Experts must know the jurisdictions in which they operate. There can be more than one.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: practitioners must know the nuances of the jurisdictions in which they operate.

cards.question: A start-up will sell its app in three new countries. What should the manager do FIRST for compliance?
options: Copy the security policy of a big competitor
Add strong encryption to the whole app
Wait until a customer sends a complaint
Learn which jurisdictions apply
options_why: Another company's policy may not match the rules that apply here.
Encryption may help, but it does not tell which rules apply.
Waiting is reactive. A manager should prevent problems.
cards.answer: Learn which jurisdictions apply
cards.explanation: She must first know who has the power to set rules. Then she can follow them.

cards.question: A company has servers in country A, an office in country B, and customers in country C. What is the BEST way to find its legal duties?
options: Study the laws of each place, plus treaties and activity
Follow only the laws of country B, where the office is
Follow the laws of the country with the fewest rules
Ask the customers which rules they prefer
options_why: The manual says geography alone is not enough.
A company cannot pick the easiest rules. The authorities decide.
Customers do not set legal rules.
cards.answer: Study the laws of each place, plus treaties and activity
cards.explanation: Jurisdiction depends on geography, treaties, and the activity of the company.

cards.question: Which statement about jurisdiction is MOST accurate?
options: It depends only on the home country of the company
It depends only on where the servers are
It can depend on treaties and on what a company does
It depends only on where the staff live
options_why: Geography alone is not enough.
The place of servers is one fact, but treaties and activity count too.
Staff location is one fact, but it does not decide alone.
cards.answer: It can depend on treaties and on what a company does
cards.explanation: The manual lists treaties, activity, and other factors, as well as geography.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Which statement about jurisdiction is NOT true?
options: It is a legal concept about official power
It can be influenced by international treaties
It can be influenced by what a company does
It is decided only by looking at a map
options_why: This is true. It is the core of the official definition.
This is true. The manual says treaties can influence it.
This is true. The activity of the organization matters.
cards.answer: It is decided only by looking at a map
cards.explanation: A map is not enough. Other factors can change who has the power.

cards.question: A security expert starts work in a new country. Which action is LEAST helpful for compliance?
options: Assuming her home rules apply there too
Learning the details of the local jurisdiction
Checking the treaties between the countries
Asking a local legal expert for advice
options_why: This is very helpful. The manual says to know the nuances.
This is helpful. Treaties can influence jurisdiction.
This is helpful. Local experts know the local rules.
cards.answer: Assuming her home rules apply there too
cards.explanation: Rules change from one place to another. A good expert checks the local jurisdiction first.

cards.question: A manager says that the company only follows the rules of the country where its head office is. What is the BEST answer?
options: Yes: the head office country always decides everything
Not always: other places and treaties can count
No: only the lawyers of the company can decide
No: customers choose the rules for the company
options_why: Geography alone is not enough.
Lawyers advise, but the legal power comes from authorities.
Customers do not make legal rules.
cards.answer: Not always: other places and treaties can count
cards.explanation: Other countries, treaties, and the company's activity can also give someone power over its rules.

cards.question: In your own words: what is jurisdiction?
cards.answer: The official power to make legal decisions in an area. It tells you who can set the rules for you.
cards.explanation: Think of the head teacher of a school.

cards.question: Besides geography, name two things that can influence jurisdiction.
cards.answer: International treaties and agreements, and the activity of the organization.
cards.explanation: The manual adds that other factors can also play a part.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “international treaties and agreements, the activity of your organization, or any number of other factors”.

cards.question: Why must a security expert know the details of each jurisdiction where they work?
cards.answer: Because rules change from one place to another. The wrong jurisdiction means the wrong rules.
cards.explanation: Same facts, other place: other rule.

cards.question: A start-up has customers in three countries. What should it do about jurisdiction?
cards.answer: Check each country. Look at the map, but also at treaties and at what the start-up does.
cards.explanation: A map is not enough.

paragraphes: The teachers vote on a rule: no phones in class. This is the big principle.
Then the head teacher writes a more exact note: phones stay switched off at the bottom of your bag. This note says how to apply the rule.
Both count. But if the note went against the voted rule, the voted rule would win. Law has two levels in the same way.

decouverte.comme: The rule voted by the teachers is the basic rule. The head teacher's note adds details, but it stays below. It cannot go against the voted rule.
decouverte.enVrai: A law is a rule that has a price if you break it. The price can be a criminal punishment, like a fine or prison. Or it can be civil liability: you must repair the harm you caused. Law has two parts. Statutes are written by the group that votes the laws. Regulations are more detailed. The picture stops here: a school note does not send anyone to a judge.

decouverte.question: A text voted by parliament and a detailed text from an agency say different things. Which one wins?
options: The text voted by parliament
The detailed text from the agency
The newest one
decouverte.explanation: Both must be followed. But the detailed text is below the voted text. It is there to apply it, not to go against it.

decouverte.texte: You read “18 U.S.C. § 1030”. It means section 1030 of title 18 of the United States Code. “C.F.R.” means the Code of Federal Regulations. In the United Kingdom, you write the name of the law, the year, then the chapter: “Computer Misuse Act 1990, c. 18”.

cards.question: Official definition: “law” (in U.S. law)
cards.answer: In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment or civil liability.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a law is a rule with a price. If you break it, you can get a criminal punishment, or you must repair the harm (civil liability).
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”. Civil liability means the duty to repair the harm done to someone.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “law” in U.S. law?
options: In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to a warning letter from the company.
In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment only.
In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment or civil liability.
In U.S. law, the word law refers to any written contract that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment or civil liability.
options_why: A warning letter is not a legal result. The sentence names criminal punishment or civil liability.
The real sentence has two results: criminal punishment or civil liability.
A contract is a deal between parties. A law is a rule from the government.
cards.answer: In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment or civil liability.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: any rule, if broken, criminal punishment or civil liability.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “law” in U.S. law from memory.
cards.answer: In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment or civil liability.
cards.explanation: Remember the order: a rule, if broken, then two possible results.

cards.question: Official definition: “statutes” and “regulations”
cards.answer: Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Statutes are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.
cards.explanation: In simple words: laws have two levels. Statutes are the main laws, written by the group that votes the laws. Regulations give more detail on how to apply a statute.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”. The legislative body is the group that votes the laws, like Congress in the United States.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “statutes” and “regulations”?
options: Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Regulations are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while statutes are more detailed rules on how the execution of a regulation will be performed.

Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Statutes are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.

Laws may be generally categorized into three parts: statutes, regulations, and contracts. Statutes are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.

Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Statutes are written and adopted by the company's board of directors (e.g., the chief executive), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.
options_why: The roles are swapped. Statutes come from the legislative body, and regulations give the detail.
The sentence names two parts only. Contracts are not a part of law here.
Statutes are adopted by the legislative body of a jurisdiction, not by a company.
cards.answer: Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Statutes are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: two parts, legislative body, and more detailed rules on how to carry out a statute.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “statutes” and “regulations” from memory.
cards.answer: Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Statutes are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: two parts, who adopts the statutes, and what regulations are for.

cards.question: Official definition: the link between “statutes” and “regulations”
cards.answer: Both statutes and regulations are legally enforceable, but regulations are subordinate to statutes.
cards.explanation: In simple words: both must be followed, but regulations sit below statutes. Subordinate means placed below.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the link between “statutes” and “regulations” from memory.
cards.answer: Both statutes and regulations are legally enforceable, but regulations are subordinate to statutes.
cards.explanation: Both are enforceable, but one sits under the other.

cards.question: A parliament votes a general rule. An agency then writes detailed steps to apply it. Which one is the regulation?
options: The general rule that parliament voted on
Both texts are regulations of the same level
Neither text is a regulation until a judge says so
The detailed steps written by the agency
options_why: That is the statute. It is adopted by the legislative body.
They are two different kinds: a statute and a regulation.
The agency's detailed steps are already the regulation.
cards.answer: The detailed steps written by the agency
cards.explanation: A regulation gives the detail of how a statute is carried out.

cards.question: A statute and a regulation say different things. Which one wins?
options: The statute, because regulations are subordinate
The regulation, because it has more detail
The newest text, even if it is a regulation
Neither, until a judge writes a new rule
options_why: More detail does not give more power. The regulation sits below the statute.
Age does not decide. The statute stays on top.
The order is already clear. Regulations are subordinate to statutes.
cards.answer: The statute, because regulations are subordinate
cards.explanation: Both are enforceable, but regulations are subordinate to statutes.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Which text is written and adopted by the legislative body?
options: A regulation
A company policy
A statute
A contract
options_why: A regulation gives the detail. It sits below the statute.
A company writes its own policy. It is not adopted by the legislative body.
A contract is a deal between parties, not a text of the legislative body.
cards.answer: A statute
cards.explanation: Statutes are written and adopted by the legislative body, like the U.S. Congress.

cards.question: A company breaks a law and must pay for the harm it caused to a customer. What is this called?
options: Criminal punishment
A regulation
A statute
Civil liability
options_why: Criminal punishment comes from the criminal justice system, such as a fine or prison. Here the company repairs harm.
A regulation is a detailed rule, not a result of breaking a law.
A statute is a written law, not the duty to repair harm.
cards.answer: Civil liability
cards.explanation: A broken law can lead to criminal punishment or civil liability. Civil liability means repairing harm.

cards.question: You read the citation “18 U.S.C. § 1030”. What does it mean?

Title 1030 of Section 18 of the United States Code
Section 1030 of Title 18 of the Code of Federal Regulations
Chapter 18 of a law written in the year 1030

C.F.R.

cards.question: Staff ask how to apply a general statute in daily work. What is the BEST source of detail?
options: Another statute, because statutes hold the details
A blog post from a security vendor
The regulations for that statute
The oldest security policy of the company

A vendor is not a legal source. The regulation is the official detail.
An old policy may not match the law.
cards.answer: The regulations for that statute
cards.explanation: Regulations are more detailed rules on how a statute will be carried out.

cards.question: Which statement about regulations is NOT true?
options: They give more details on how to apply a statute
They are only advice and cannot be enforced
They are legally enforceable
They are subordinate to statutes

This is true. Both statutes and regulations are enforceable.

A contract signed by two companies

A law voted by the U.S. Congress

A company policy is not adopted by the legislative body.

Year, then the name of the judge
Chapter, then title, then name of the agency

cards.question: A statute forbids sharing a type of data. An agency regulation seems to allow it. What is the BEST way to act?
options: Follow the regulation, because it is more detailed
Follow whichever rule costs the company less
Follow the statute, because the regulation is subordinate
Do nothing until a judge decides the case
options_why: Detail does not win. The regulation cannot go against the statute.
A company cannot pick by cost. It must satisfy the rules.
Waiting is risky. The order of the two texts is already clear.
cards.answer: Follow the statute, because the regulation is subordinate
cards.explanation: Regulations are subordinate to statutes. So the statute wins.

cards.question: What are laws for, according to the manual?
cards.answer: To say what is allowed and what is not.
cards.explanation: A law draws the line between what you can do and what you cannot do.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: In your own words: why do we need regulations as well as statutes?
cards.answer: A statute sets the main principle. Regulations give the details of how to apply it.
cards.explanation: Without details, it would be hard to know what to do in practice.

cards.question: In your own words: what is the difference between criminal punishment and civil liability?
cards.answer: Criminal punishment comes from the criminal justice system, like a fine or prison. Civil liability means you must repair the harm done to someone.
cards.explanation: Both can follow the breaking of a law.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: a broken law leads to criminal punishment or civil liability. The plain explanation is outside the manual.

cards.question: A colleague says: “A regulation is only advice.” What do you answer?
cards.answer: No. A regulation is a detailed rule with legal force. It is enforceable like a statute, but it sits below it.
cards.explanation: Advice does not oblige anyone. A regulation does.

paragraphes: Karim arrives late. He gets a one-hour detention.
Lina forges her school report. She goes before the discipline board.
A school ranks mistakes by how serious they are. The law does the same. In the United States, two words come up all the time: misdemeanor and felony.

decouverte.comme: A detention is for a small slip. An expulsion is for a serious fault. The heavier the fault, the heavier the punishment.
decouverte.enVrai: U.S. law ranks criminal offenses in the same way. A misdemeanor is a lighter offense. A felony is a more serious offense with heavier penalties. The picture stops here: these are not school punishments, but levels in the justice system.

decouverte.question: In the United States, from how many months of possible prison do we talk about a felony?
options: More than 6 months
More than 12 months
More than 5 years
decouverte.explanation: The manual puts the line at 12 months. Below it, the offense is a misdemeanor. Above it, it is a felony.

decouverte.texte: Other countries use other words. In France, Germany, and Switzerland, serious offenses are called crimes. Less serious ones are called misdemeanors or delicts. A delict is a less serious offense. Brazil uses the word contravention.

cards.question: Official definition: “misdemeanor”
cards.answer: In U.S. law, a misdemeanor is any "lesser" criminal act that is punishable by less than 12 months in prison.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a misdemeanor is a lighter crime. The possible prison time is less than 12 months.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Legal and Regulatory Issues”.

cards.question: Official definition: “felony”
cards.answer: A felony, under U.S. law, is a more serious criminal offense that carries more serious penalties, including jail time over 12 months (and as high as one's lifetime).

cards.answer: A felony, under U.S. law, is a more serious criminal offense that carries more serious penalties, including jail time over 12 months (and as high as one's lifetime).
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: more serious, more serious penalties, and over 12 months.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “felony” from memory.

cards.explanation: Remember: more serious, heavier penalties, over 12 months, up to a lifetime.

options: A felony

A statute

A statute is a written law, not a level of offense.

decouverte.titre: One set of rules for every office
paragraphes: The government has thousands of computers. They hold sensitive files about citizens.
If every office makes its own protection rules, some will be well protected and others will not.
So a law sets a minimum for all. In the United States, the first one is the Computer Security Act of 1987. In 2002, a new law replaced it: FISMA.

decouverte.comme: The education ministry sets a safety minimum for all schools: locked doors and a visitors' book. A school can do better, but never less.
decouverte.enVrai: The Computer Security Act asks for minimum security practices on the computers of the federal government. Federal means the central government of the United States. It also asks each agency to have policies that follow these practices. FISMA, in 2002, takes the idea and goes further. The picture stops here: the 1987 law is for government computers, not for all companies.

decouverte.question: A government computer holds ordinary information. It is not secret and not military. Who sets its security standards?
options: NIST, a standards institute
The NSA, the national security agency
Congress, the parliament
decouverte.explanation: NIST sets standards for systems that are not secret and not military. The NSA takes care of secret (classified) and military systems.

decouverte.titre: A company that works for the government
decouverte.texte: A private company runs the website of a federal agency. It is not an agency itself. FISMA still applies to it, because it provides information services to the agency. It must do security assessments based on risk, using the NIST method.

cards.question: Official definition: “FISMA”
cards.answer: The Federal Information Security Management Act, commonly referred to as FISMA (pronounced "fizz-muh"), is a U.S. law enacted in 2002 that greatly extends the Computer Security Act of 1987.
cards.explanation: In simple words: FISMA is a U.S. law from 2002. It builds on the Computer Security Act of 1987 and goes much further.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) of 2002”. Federal means: from the central government of the United States.

cards.question: Official definition: what FISMA requires
cards.answer: FISMA acknowledges the importance of information security to the United States' economic and national security interests and requires that all U.S. federal government agencies and nongovernment organizations that provide information services to these agencies conduct risk-based security assessments that align with the NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF).
cards.explanation: In simple words: agencies, and the companies that work for them, must assess their security based on risk. They follow the NIST method (RMF).
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) of 2002”. RMF stands for Risk Management Framework: the NIST framework for managing risks.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about what FISMA requires from memory.

cards.question: Official definition: the “Computer Security Act”
cards.answer: The Computer Security Act was enacted by the U.S. Congress in 1987 with the objective of improving the security and privacy of sensitive information stored on U.S. federal government computers.

cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Computer Security Act of 1987”.

cards.question: Official definition: the roles of NIST and the NSA under the Computer Security Act
cards.answer: The Computer Security Act establishes that the National Institute for Standards and Technology, an agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce, is responsible for setting computer security standards for unclassified, nonmilitary government computer systems, while the National Security Agency (NSA) is responsible for setting security guidance for classified government and military systems and applications.
cards.explanation: In simple words: NIST handles standards for ordinary government systems. The NSA handles secret and military systems.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Computer Security Act of 1987”. Classified means declared secret by the government.

cards.question: What does FISMA stand for?
cards.answer: Federal Information Security Management Act.
cards.explanation: The M is for Management.

cards.question: In which years were the Computer Security Act and FISMA passed?
cards.answer: 1987 for the Computer Security Act, 2002 for FISMA.
cards.explanation: FISMA is the more recent one. It repealed the 1987 act.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1.

cards.question: What did the Computer Security Act ask for on federal government computers?
cards.answer: Minimum acceptable security practices, and policies so that agencies follow them.
cards.explanation: A minimum for everyone, like common rules for all schools.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Computer Security Act of 1987”.

cards.question: What does RMF stand for?
cards.answer: Risk Management Framework. It is the NIST framework for managing risk.
cards.explanation: FISMA asks agencies to align their assessments with it.

paragraphes: Your sports club sells shares to its fans. The treasurer says all is fine.
In truth, he hides the losses so that fans keep buying. When the truth comes out, nobody trusts the club.
In the United States, big accounting scandals happened in real companies. In 2002, a law was passed to rebuild trust: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX).

decouverte.comme: For fans to trust the club, it must be open. The treasurer cannot decide on spending that helps himself. That is a conflict of interest. The accounts are checked. If he lies, he is punished. Anyone who finds cheating can report it safely.
decouverte.enVrai: SOX asks the same of publicly traded companies. These are companies whose shares anyone can buy. They must set up controls, give investors information about risks, and punish executives who lie. They must also protect whistleblowers. A whistleblower reports wrongdoing to regulators, the authorities that watch over an industry. The picture stops here: SOX is for big companies, not for your club.

decouverte.question: SOX is a law about company money. Does it have a link with computers and IT?
options: No, no link at all
Yes, a real and growing link
Yes, but only for companies in the IT industry
decouverte.answer: Yes, a real and growing link
decouverte.explanation: The manual says SOX is mainly financial. But its impact on IT and security is real and growing.

decouverte.titre: The numbers of a store chain
decouverte.texte: A big store chain is listed on the stock market. Its sales figures go through accounting software. If an employee could change them without a trace, the official accounts (the financial statements) could not be trusted. So auditors, the outside checkers, also look at who can use this software.

cards.question: Official definition: why the “SOX” law was passed
cards.answer: Following several high-profile corporate and accounting scandals, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reestablish public trust in publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
cards.explanation: In simple words: after big accounting scandals, the U.S. passed SOX to win back public trust in listed companies and accounting firms.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”. A publicly traded company is a company whose shares anyone can buy.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official explanation of why SOX was passed?
options: Following several high-profile corporate and accounting scandals, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reduce the cost of audits in publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
Following several high-profile data breaches and cyberattacks, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reestablish public trust in publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
Following several high-profile corporate and accounting scandals, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reestablish public trust in banks and insurance companies.
Following several high-profile corporate and accounting scandals, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reestablish public trust in publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
options_why: SOX aimed to rebuild public trust, not to cut audit costs.
SOX came from accounting scandals, not from cyberattacks.
SOX covers publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
cards.answer: Following several high-profile corporate and accounting scandals, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reestablish public trust in publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: scandals, reestablish public trust, and publicly traded companies.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about why SOX was passed from memory.
cards.answer: Following several high-profile corporate and accounting scandals, the SOX was enacted in the United States to reestablish public trust in publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the scandals, the goal, and the publicly traded companies.

cards.question: Official definition: what SOX required of companies
cards.answer: SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to minimize conflicts of interest, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil and criminal penalties on executives for providing false financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.
cards.explanation: In simple words: four ideas. Avoid conflicts of interest, tell investors about risks, punish executives who lie, and protect whistleblowers.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”. Executives are the leaders of the company. Investors are people who buy shares.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official statement of what SOX required of companies?
options: SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to minimize conflicts of interest, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil and criminal penalties on executives for providing false financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.

SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to maximize profits for shareholders, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil and criminal penalties on executives for providing false financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.

SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to minimize conflicts of interest, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil penalties on auditors for providing late financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.

SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to minimize conflicts of interest, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil and criminal penalties on executives for providing false financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to the press.
options_why: The SOX controls aim to minimize conflicts of interest, not to raise profits.
The penalties are civil and criminal, and they target executives who give false disclosures.
The whistleblowers in the sentence report to regulators, not to the press.
cards.answer: SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to minimize conflicts of interest, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil and criminal penalties on executives for providing false financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.
cards.explanation: Look at the four ideas: conflicts of interest, risk information, penalties for executives, and protection for whistleblowers.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about what SOX required of companies from memory.
cards.answer: SOX required companies to implement a wide range of controls intended to minimize conflicts of interest, provide investors with appropriate risk information, place civil and criminal penalties on executives for providing false financial disclosures, and provide protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.
cards.explanation: Remember the four ideas in order: conflicts, risks, penalties, whistleblowers.

cards.question: Official definition: the “PCAOB”
cards.answer: Under SOX, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) was established as a nonprofit organization responsible for overseeing the implementation of SOX.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the PCAOB is a nonprofit group that watches over how SOX is applied.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”. Nonprofit means it does not try to make money.

cards.question: Say the official definition of the “PCAOB” from memory.
cards.answer: Under SOX, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) was established as a nonprofit organization responsible for overseeing the implementation of SOX.
cards.explanation: Its name, its nature (nonprofit), and its job (overseeing SOX).

cards.question: Official definition: the PCAOB's “Auditing Standards”
cards.answer: PCAOB's "Auditing Standards" identify the role that information systems play in maintaining financial records and requires auditors to assess the use of IT as it relates to maintaining and preparing financial statements.
cards.explanation: In simple words: auditors must also look at the computer systems that keep and prepare the accounts.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”. IT stands for information technology.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about the PCAOB's Auditing Standards from memory.
cards.answer: PCAOB's "Auditing Standards" identify the role that information systems play in maintaining financial records and requires auditors to assess the use of IT as it relates to maintaining and preparing financial statements.
cards.explanation: The role of the systems, the financial records, and the work of the auditors.

cards.question: Why was SOX passed in the United States?
options: To stop cyberattacks on government computers
To rebuild public trust after accounting scandals
To set rules for personal data
To make audits cheaper for companies
options_why: That is closer to FISMA. SOX came from accounting scandals.
Rules for personal data are about privacy, a different topic.
The goal was trust, not lower costs.
cards.answer: To rebuild public trust after accounting scandals
cards.explanation: SOX was enacted after several big corporate and accounting scandals, to reestablish public trust.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”.

cards.question: Who does SOX protect when they report wrongdoing to regulators?
options: An executive
A supplier
A whistleblower
An investor
options_why: Executives face penalties if they give false figures. They are not the ones protected here.
The protection is for people who report wrongdoing.
Investors receive risk information, but the protection is for those who report.
cards.answer: A whistleblower
cards.explanation: SOX protects whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.

cards.question: SOX is mainly which kind of law?
options: A privacy law for patient records
A mostly financial law with an IT impact
A law about card payment security
A law only for companies that make software
options_why: Privacy for personal data is a different topic.
Card payment rules come from a standard that you will meet later.
SOX targets public companies and accounting firms in any field.
cards.answer: A mostly financial law with an IT impact
cards.explanation: SOX is largely a financial law. Its impact on IT and security is real and growing.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”.

cards.question: Who oversees the implementation of SOX?
options: NIST
The NSA
The U.S. Congress
The PCAOB
options_why: NIST sets standards for government computers.
The NSA handles classified and military systems.
Congress passed the law. A nonprofit board oversees it.
cards.answer: The PCAOB
cards.explanation: The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) oversees the implementation of SOX.

cards.question: An accounting manager approves her own spending. Which SOX control BEST fits this problem?
options: Controls to minimize conflicts of interest
Protection for any employee who reports cheating
Civil and criminal penalties for senior executives
Clear risk information given to the investors
options_why: That helps people who report cheating. It does not stop the conflict itself.
Penalties come after false disclosures, not for a conflict of interest.
That is about telling investors about risks.
cards.answer: Controls to minimize conflicts of interest
cards.explanation: Approving your own spending is a conflict of interest. SOX required controls to minimize it.

cards.question: A listed company keeps its sales numbers in accounting software. What is the BEST reason for auditors to check who can change it?
options: SOX says that every program must have a license
SOX is mainly an IT law, so IT comes before accounts
A hidden change could distort the accounts
Auditors want to read all of the program code
options_why: SOX is not about software licenses.
SOX is mainly financial. Its IT impact comes from the accounts.
The concern is who can change the numbers, not the code.
cards.answer: A hidden change could distort the accounts
cards.explanation: False numbers can come from a poorly controlled system. So auditors must assess the use of IT for the accounts.

cards.question: Which executive action is MOST likely to bring civil and criminal penalties under SOX?
options: Reporting a fraud to the regulators
Delaying a software upgrade for a few months
Hiring an outside auditor to check the accounts
Giving false financial disclosures
options_why: That is a whistleblower action, and SOX protects it.
That is not what SOX penalizes. It targets false financial disclosures.
Auditors are part of the SOX system. Hiring one is normal.
cards.answer: Giving false financial disclosures
cards.explanation: SOX places civil and criminal penalties on executives who give false financial disclosures.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a control that SOX required?
options: Rules to protect payment card data
Controls to minimize conflicts of interest
Giving investors the appropriate risk information
Protections for whistleblowers who report to regulators
options_why: True: SOX required this.
True: SOX required this.
True: SOX required this.
cards.answer: Rules to protect payment card data
cards.explanation: Rules for payment card data come from another standard that you will meet soon.

cards.question: Which organization is LEAST likely to be a target of SOX?
options: A company whose shares anyone can buy
A small shop whose shares nobody can buy
A public accounting firm
A listed chain of stores with a big IT team
options_why: That is a publicly traded company, the main target of SOX.
Public accounting firms are named in the law.
Listed companies are covered, with or without a big IT team.
cards.answer: A small shop whose shares nobody can buy
cards.explanation: SOX targets publicly traded companies and public accounting firms.

cards.question: An IT director says that SOX is only a law for accountants. What is the BEST answer?
options: You are right: IT is never part of an audit
SOX is only for IT staff, not for accountants
SOX is financial first, with a real IT impact
SOX applies only to companies that make software
options_why: Auditors must assess the use of IT for the accounts.
SOX is mainly financial, so it is not only for IT staff.
It applies to publicly traded companies in any field.
cards.answer: SOX is financial first, with a real IT impact
cards.explanation: SOX is largely a financial law. Its impact on IT and information security is real and growing.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”.

cards.question: A worker sees her boss hide a loss and tells the regulators. What does SOX give her?
options: A bonus paid by the PCAOB
Protection as a whistleblower
Nothing, because only executives are covered
A new job at another company
options_why: The manual does not mention a bonus. It mentions protection.
SOX also protects whistleblowers, so she is covered.
The manual speaks of protection, not of a new job.
cards.answer: Protection as a whistleblower
cards.explanation: SOX required protections for whistleblowers who report inappropriate actions to regulators.

cards.question: What does PCAOB stand for?
cards.answer: Public Company Accounting Oversight Board: the nonprofit group that oversees SOX.
cards.explanation: Oversight means watching over. It is the watchdog of SOX.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”.

cards.question: What is the full name of SOX, and in which year was it passed?
cards.answer: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002.
cards.explanation: It dates from the same year as FISMA.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “U.S. Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002”.

cards.question: In your own words: why does a finance law like SOX matter for IT?
cards.answer: The accounts are kept and prepared with computer systems. A weak system or a hidden change could make the numbers false.
cards.explanation: If the systems cannot be trusted, the accounts cannot either.

cards.question: What does SOX do to protect people who report fraud?
cards.answer: It protects whistleblowers, people who report wrongdoing to regulators.
cards.explanation: Without this protection, many people would stay silent.

paragraphes: Your club wants to use the payment service of a small company. You ask: “Is your service safe?”
They answer: “Yes, trust us.” That is not enough for you. You want proof from an outside checker.
In the business world, this proof exists: the SOC audit report. An audit is a check done by a specialist, who then writes a report.

decouverte.titre: A detailed report card and a displayed certificate
decouverte.comme: At the end of the year, your parents get a detailed report with all the comments. The school only shows a short certificate at the entrance, without the details.
decouverte.enVrai: A SOC 2 report is the detailed report. It goes to customers and trusted parties. A SOC 3 report is the short certificate. It is public and hides sensitive details. A SOC 1 report is another document, about money. The picture stops here: a report card grades a student, but a SOC report checks an organization.

decouverte.question: A company wants to show everyone on its website that it is serious. It does not want to share its secrets. Which report does it publish?
options: A SOC 1 report
A SOC 2 report
A SOC 3 report
decouverte.explanation: SOC 3 is a lighter version, without sensitive details. SOC 2 is kept for trusted parties.

decouverte.texte: A company processes card payments for hundreds of shops. Its numbers affect its customers' official accounts. It will probably need a SOC 1 report. It can also show a SOC 2 report to customers and regulators.

cards.question: Official definition: “SOC”
cards.answer: Often confused with SOX (discussed previously), SOC stands for System and Organization Controls and is an auditing framework that gives organizations the flexibility to be audited based on their own needs.
cards.explanation: In simple words: SOC is a flexible way to audit a company. It is not a law. SOC is often confused with SOX, which is a law.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “SOC” from memory.
cards.answer: Often confused with SOX (discussed previously), SOC stands for System and Organization Controls and is an auditing framework that gives organizations the flexibility to be audited based on their own needs.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the full name, the nature (an audit framework), and the flexibility.

cards.question: Official definition: “SOC 1”
cards.answer: SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses strictly on a company's financial statements and controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.
cards.explanation: In simple words: SOC 1 is a report about money. It looks at the company's financial statements and the controls that touch its customers' accounts.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”. The manual adds that a company that processes credit cards is likely to need a SOC 1 report.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “SOC 1”?
options: SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses strictly on a company's privacy practices and controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.
SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses loosely on a company's financial statements and controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.
SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses strictly on a company's financial statements and controls that can impact a customer's website speed.
SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses strictly on a company's financial statements and controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.
options_why: SOC 1 is about financial statements, not privacy practices.
The word is strictly. SOC 1 stays on financial statements.
SOC 1 is about a customer's financial statements.
cards.answer: SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses strictly on a company's financial statements and controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: strictly, financial statements, and a customer's financial statements.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “SOC 1” from memory.
cards.answer: SOC 1: An audit and compliance report that focuses strictly on a company's financial statements and controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.
cards.explanation: Strictly about the company's accounts, and their effect on the customer's accounts.

cards.question: Official definition: “SOC 2”
cards.answer: SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on AICPA's five "Trust Services principles": privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.
cards.explanation: In simple words: SOC 2 is the detailed security report. It checks five trust principles: privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”. AICPA stands for American Institute of Certified Public Accountants.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “SOC 2”?
options: SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on AICPA's five "Trust Services principles": privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.
SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on AICPA's three "Trust Services principles": security, availability, and confidentiality.
SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on AICPA's five "Trust Services principles": privacy, security, availability, nonrepudiation, and confidentiality.
SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on ISO's five "Trust Services principles": privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.
options_why: SOC 2 has five principles, not three. Privacy and processing integrity are two of them.
Processing integrity is one of the five. Nonrepudiation is not.
The principles come from the AICPA, the American institute of accountants.
cards.answer: SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on AICPA's five "Trust Services principles": privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: evaluates, the AICPA, five Trust Services principles, and the list of five.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “SOC 2” from memory.
cards.answer: SOC 2: An audit and compliance report that evaluates an organization based on AICPA's five "Trust Services principles": privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the AICPA and its five principles, split into two lists.

cards.question: Official definition: “SOC 3”
cards.answer: SOC 3: This is a "lite" version of a SOC 2 report and abstracts or removes all sensitive details.
cards.explanation: In simple words: SOC 3 is the short public version of SOC 2. It hides the sensitive details.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”. The manual says companies make SOC 3 reports public and keep SOC 2 reports for trusted parties.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “SOC 3”?
options: SOC 3: This is a "lite" version of a SOC 1 report and abstracts or removes all sensitive details.
SOC 3: This is a "full" version of a SOC 2 report and abstracts or removes all sensitive details.
SOC 3: This is a "lite" version of a SOC 2 report and abstracts or removes all sensitive details.
SOC 3: This is a "lite" version of a SOC 2 report and abstracts or removes some sensitive details.
options_why: SOC 3 is the lite version of a SOC 2 report.
SOC 3 is the lite version. The full detail is in SOC 2.
The word is all. SOC 3 hides all sensitive details.
cards.answer: SOC 3: This is a "lite" version of a SOC 2 report and abstracts or removes all sensitive details.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: lite, a version of SOC 2, and all sensitive details.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “SOC 3” from memory.
cards.answer: SOC 3: This is a "lite" version of a SOC 2 report and abstracts or removes all sensitive details.
cards.explanation: A lighter version of SOC 2, with all the sensitive details removed.

cards.question: Which report focuses strictly on a company's financial statements?
options: SOC 2
SOC 3
SOX
SOC 1
options_why: SOC 2 looks at five trust principles, not only at financial statements.
SOC 3 is the lite public version of SOC 2.
SOX is a law, not an audit report.
cards.answer: SOC 1
cards.explanation: SOC 1 is about the financial statements and the controls that can impact a customer's financial statements.

cards.question: Which report is the lite version that can be shared with the public?
options: SOC 3
SOC 1
SOC 2
None, all SOC reports must stay private
options_why: SOC 1 is about financial statements. It is not the public one.
SOC 2 has sensitive details, so it is kept for trusted parties.
SOC 3 is made to be public, because it hides the sensitive details.
cards.answer: SOC 3
cards.explanation: SOC 3 removes the sensitive details, so companies can make it available to the public.

cards.question: SOC and SOX sound alike. What is the difference?
options: SOC is a law, while SOX is an audit framework
SOC is an audit framework, but SOX is a law
Both are laws about card payments
They are two names for the same law
options_why: It is the other way round.
Neither one is about card payments. SOX is a financial law.
SOC is an audit framework. SOX is a law. People often confuse them.
cards.answer: SOC is an audit framework, but SOX is a law
cards.explanation: SOC stands for System and Organization Controls. It is an auditing framework, not a law.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”.

cards.question: Which of these is one of the five Trust Services principles?
options: Authentication of every user
Accountability for every action
Processing integrity
Efficiency of the audit work
options_why: Authentication is a security idea, but it is not one of the five.
Accountability is not one of the five.
Efficiency is not one of the five.
cards.answer: Processing integrity
cards.explanation: The five are privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality.

cards.question: A company wants to show trusted customers the details of its security and availability controls. Which report is BEST?
options: A SOC 1 report
A SOC 2 report
A SOC 3 report
A PCAOB report
options_why: SOC 1 focuses on financial statements, not on security.
SOC 3 hides the details. These customers want the details.
The PCAOB oversees SOX. It is not a SOC report.
cards.answer: A SOC 2 report
cards.explanation: SOC 2 evaluates the five trust principles and gives the detailed results to trusted parties.

cards.question: A company wants to show the public that it meets the trust principles. It will not share its secrets. Which report is BEST?
options: A SOC 2 report
A SOC 1 report
A copy of its internal security policy
A SOC 3 report
options_why: SOC 2 is kept for trusted parties, because it has sensitive details.
SOC 1 is about financial statements.
An internal policy may reveal secrets. SOC 3 is made for the public.
cards.answer: A SOC 3 report
cards.explanation: SOC 3 says if each principle is met, without giving the specific details.

cards.question: A company processes credit card payments for shops. Which report is it MOST likely to need?
options: A SOC 1 report
A SOC 3 report
A SOC 2 report
A FISMA assessment
options_why: SOC 3 is a public summary of SOC 2. It is not about the shops' financial statements.
SOC 2 is about trust principles. The manual links card processing to SOC 1.
FISMA is a U.S. law for federal agencies, not a SOC report.
cards.answer: A SOC 1 report
cards.explanation: A company that performs credit card processing is likely to need a SOC 1 report.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the five Trust Services principles?
options: Privacy
Availability
Nonrepudiation
Confidentiality
options_why: Privacy is one of the five principles.
Availability is one of the five principles.
Confidentiality is one of the five principles.
cards.answer: Nonrepudiation
cards.explanation: The five are privacy, security, availability, processing integrity, and confidentiality. Nonrepudiation means a person cannot deny what they did.

cards.question: Which report shows the LEAST detail about a company's controls?
options: SOC 2
SOC 1
All three show the same detail
SOC 3
options_why: SOC 2 gives the detailed results of the controls.
SOC 1 gives details about controls that touch financial statements.
SOC 3 is the lite one. It removes sensitive details.
cards.answer: SOC 3
cards.explanation: SOC 3 is a lite version of SOC 2. It removes all the sensitive details.

cards.question: Which organization published the SSAE 18 standard that SOC reports follow, and when?
options: The AICPA, in 2017
NIST, in 2017
The AICPA, in 2007
The PCAOB, in 2002
options_why: NIST sets standards for government computers. The AICPA published SSAE 18.
The year is 2017. SSAE 20 changed it in 2019.
The PCAOB oversees SOX. SSAE 18 came from the AICPA in 2017.
cards.answer: The AICPA, in 2017
cards.explanation: SSAE stands for Statement on Standards for Attestation Engagements. SSAE 18 came out in 2017 and SSAE 20 changed it in 2019.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”.

cards.question: Why can a SOC 3 report be public, while a SOC 2 report is kept for trusted parties?
options: SOC 3 is shorter, so it costs less to print
SOC 3 removes all the sensitive details
A SOC 2 report is a law, so it must stay private
SOC 3 covers only the financial statements
options_why: Length is not the reason. Sensitive details are.
SOC 2 is an audit report, not a law.
SOC 3 covers the same principles as SOC 2, without the sensitive details.
cards.answer: SOC 3 removes all the sensitive details
cards.explanation: A SOC 3 report says if the principles are met without giving the specific details. A SOC 2 report has those details.

cards.question: What does SOC stand for?
cards.answer: System and Organization Controls.
cards.explanation: It is an audit framework, not a law.

cards.question: Who gets a SOC 2 report, and who can get a SOC 3 report?
cards.answer: A SOC 2 report goes to trusted parties, like customers and regulators. A SOC 3 report can be public.
cards.explanation: Think of the detailed report and the displayed certificate.

cards.question: In your own words: when does a company need a SOC 1 report?
cards.answer: When its controls can affect its customers' financial statements, for example a company that processes credit card payments.
cards.explanation: Its figures affect its customers' accounts.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “System and Organization Controls”.

cards.question: What does AICPA stand for?
cards.answer: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. SOC reports follow its standard, SSAE 18.
cards.explanation: It is the American institute of accountants.

concepts.name: The PCI DSS standard (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)

cards.question: Official definition: “PCI DSS”
cards.answer: PCI DSS is a proprietary security standard established in 2004. cards.explanation: In simple words: PCI DSS is the security rulebook for card payments. It covers shops, payment services, and the makers of payment software and devices.
